title: Build words with -tion
summary: Connect spelling, meaning and word families: action, connection, detection and protection. Text-based practice; no listening assessment.
objectives: Spell four useful -tion nouns without fuzzy matching.
Connect act, connect, detect and protect with their noun forms.
Use the nouns in a short, self-reviewed security note.
prerequisites: Everyday spoken English; no assumption about your writing level.

teaching.title: 1 · Notice the family (4 minutes)
teaching.body: A word family links related words. In this small group, add ion to a verb ending in t: act → action; connect → connection; detect → detection; protect → protection. The noun names an act, process or result. Learn these four pairs; this is not a rule for every English verb. The BBC source explains why the sound alone does not tell you whether to write tion, sion or tian.

teaching.title: 2 · Work through a spelling (4 minutes)
teaching.body: Worked example: “The firewall helps with the ___ of the network.” The meaning is keeping something safe. Start with protect. Keep every letter: protect + ion = protection. Do not write “protecion”: the t belongs to the base. Compare detect + ion = detection. Do not add an extra t. Read the whole word, cover it, write it, then compare.

teaching.title: 3 · Break it down, then use it (3 minutes)
teaching.body: For writing, use meaningful chunks: connect + ion and protect + ion. These are spelling chunks, not pronunciation marks. A syllable is a spoken beat, which differs from a spelling chunk. Connection has three syllables in the Cambridge UK model; its final tion is one syllable. This guidance is for awareness, not a test of your Australian accent. No accent scoring or listening claim is made here. Context helps: a connection links devices; detection finds a problem; protection helps prevent harm; an action is something you do. Australian English uses these spellings too.

teaching.title: 4 · Practise, apply, review (14 minutes)
teaching.body: Spend about 8 minutes on the six practice items, 4 minutes on your own note, then 2 minutes on the review. Try before opening a hint. Hints build towards the answer; full solutions are a separate action. Completion requires every precise answer to be correct and your note to be explicitly self-reviewed. A solution-assisted finish is recorded and does not prove independent mastery.

tasks.prompt: Build the noun: act + ion. Write the whole word.
hints: Look at the related base word and the sentence meaning.
Keep the base spelling and check the ending letter by letter.
tasks.explanation: Act keeps its t: act + ion = action. “Acttion” doubles a letter that is already present.
tasks.feedback: Check whether you doubled the final t. The base word already ends in t; add only ion.

tasks.prompt: Build the noun from connect: “Check the network ___.”
hints: Look at the related base word and the sentence meaning.
Keep the base spelling and check the ending letter by letter.
tasks.explanation: Connect + ion = connection. Keep both n letters from connect; “conection” loses one.
tasks.feedback: Check both n letters in the base word. A link between devices needs the noun form of connect.

tasks.prompt: Build the noun from detect: “Early ___ helps us find problems.”
hints: Look at the related base word and the sentence meaning.
Keep the base spelling and check the ending letter by letter.
tasks.explanation: Detect + ion = detection. The t remains before ion; “detecion” loses it.
tasks.feedback: Keep the complete base detect, including its last t. Add ion without inserting another t.

tasks.prompt: Build the noun from protect: “A helmet provides ___.”
hints: Look at the related base word and the sentence meaning.
Keep the base spelling and check the ending letter by letter.
tasks.explanation: Protect + ion = protection. A helmet reduces harm: the context means keeping someone safe.
tasks.feedback: Keep the final t from protect. The sentence describes keeping someone safe, so use the noun form.

tasks.prompt: Choose connection or detection: “The alert led to the ___ of unusual traffic.”
hints: Look at the related base word and the sentence meaning.
Keep the base spelling and check the ending letter by letter.
tasks.explanation: Detection means finding something. Connection means a link, which does not fit this sentence.
tasks.feedback: An alert helps you find something. Choose the noun for finding a problem rather than linking devices.

tasks.prompt: Correct the spelling of one word: “The conection failed.” Write only the corrected word.
hints: Look at the related base word and the sentence meaning.
Keep the base spelling and check the ending letter by letter.
tasks.explanation: Connection keeps connect intact and adds ion. Check con + nect + ion rather than guessing from sound.
tasks.feedback: The sentence already has the right meaning. Check for a missing n and keep the complete base connect.

tasks.prompt: Write 2–3 sentences about a lost network connection and a sensible next action. Use connection and action; use detection or protection if it fits. Then compare your note with the rubric.
hints: Look at the related base word and the sentence meaning.
Keep the base spelling and check the ending letter by letter.
tasks.explanation: There are many valid notes. A written answer is not automatically marked correct. Review meaning and spelling yourself.
tasks.example: The connection stopped during the update. My next action is to check the cable. I will keep firewall protection enabled.
rubric: Use connection and action with the intended meaning.
Check each target word against its base + ion.
languageChecklist: Use complete sentences with capitals and full stops.
Keep the sequence clear; avoid claiming certainty without evidence.
tasks.feedback: Use the rubric to review meaning and spelling. Your writing is self-assessed, not automatically marked correct.

tasks.prompt: Without looking back, build the noun from protect.
hints: Look at the related base word and the sentence meaning.
Keep the base spelling and check the ending letter by letter.
tasks.explanation: Review the family: protect → protection. Revisit the worked example if you omitted t.
tasks.feedback: Recall the whole base word protect. Keep its last letter before adding ion.

sources.title: BBC Learning English: Suffixes -tian, -sion, -tion
sources.supports: Suffixes can change word form and meaning; several spellings share an ending sound. Supports attention to word families rather than guessing spelling from sound alone.

sources.supports: UK pronunciation model supports three syllables in connection and a single final syllable. British dictionary reference, not an Australian accent standard.

title: Investigate a suspicious HTTP check-in
summary: A 60-minute evidence investigation using a tiny synthetic PCAP. Inspect hosts, requests and timing, then write a careful incident summary.
objectives: Identify hosts and isolate HTTP requests with display filters.
Follow a TCP conversation and cite frames and timestamps.
Separate observed traffic from an unproven compromise claim.
prerequisites: Basic TCP/IP, Linux and security knowledge.
Desktop: install Wireshark from wireshark.org. No live capture or elevated capture permissions are needed. Mobile: use the bundled evidence summary for review.

teaching.title: 1 · Scope and setup (10 minutes)
teaching.body: This is a harmless synthetic simulation, generated locally with documentation-only IP addresses and a .test hostname. It is not malware or a real incident. Download check-in.pcap and open it with File → Open in Wireshark. Do not browse to the captured host. Start with Statistics → Conversations → IPv4 and note the endpoints. Set View → Time Display Format → UTC Date and Time of Day to compare the evidence times. The supplied browser evidence table supports mobile review; full Wireshark practice is a desktop activity.

teaching.title: 2 · Guided filter example (10 minutes)
teaching.body: First apply tcp, then http.request in the display filter bar. Filters change the view, not the capture. A worked comparison: ip.addr == 192.0.2.10 selects packets to or from the workstation; ip.src == 192.0.2.10 selects its outgoing packets only. Record how many requests remain under http.request. Inspect the source, destination, Host and Request URI fields. Use the frame number as an evidence reference.

teaching.title: 3 · Examine a stream (10 minutes)
teaching.body: Select frame 4, then Analyze → Follow → TCP Stream. Read the request and response together. Close the window; the stream display filter may remain, so clear it before counting all requests. Record the method, URI, Host and response body. A successful HTTP status only tells you about that exchange; it does not prove a machine is healthy or infected. The short body is plain text, not executable content.

teaching.title: 4 · Test a hypothesis (15 minutes)
teaching.body: Compare the request timestamps. Repeated check-ins can resemble automated polling, but regular timing is not proof of malware: legitimate monitoring also polls. These three requests all share one TCP connection. Use frame.time_epoch or UTC time for precise timing; do not confuse the connection handshake with the first request. Independently find the third request frame and calculate the gap between consecutive requests. Keep observations separate from hypotheses.

teaching.title: 5 · Communicate and review (15 minutes)
teaching.body: Write a short incident summary for a colleague: scope, host pair, request pattern, frame/time evidence, uncertainty and next evidence to collect. Suggest checking process ownership and endpoint logs; this PCAP alone cannot establish the process or malware identity. Complete the technical self-review and language checklist explicitly. Finish by reviewing what the capture can and cannot prove. Precise tasks must be correct; the written report is self-assessed, never AI graded.

tasks.prompt: With http.request applied, what IPv4 address sends the requests?
hints: Inspect the Source column on an HTTP request.
Frame 4 is the first request; distinguish source from destination.
tasks.explanation: Frames 4, 6 and 8 originate at 192.0.2.10. The responder is 198.51.100.20.
tasks.feedback: Read Source on a request frame, not on a response. Enter an IPv4 address rather than a hostname.

tasks.prompt: What IPv4 address receives the HTTP requests?
hints: Inspect the Destination column rather than the Host header.
Use frame 4 and read the IPv4 destination.
tasks.explanation: The requests target 198.51.100.20 on TCP port 80. This documentation address is not a live threat indicator.
tasks.feedback: Read Destination on an HTTP request. The Host header is a name, not the destination IPv4 address.

tasks.prompt: How many frames match http.request after you clear any stream filter? Write a number.
hints: Apply only http.request to the whole file.
Count requests, not HTTP responses or handshake packets.
tasks.explanation: Frames 4, 6 and 8 contain the three complete HTTP requests.
tasks.feedback: Clear the stream filter, apply only http.request and count displayed request frames. Do not count responses.

tasks.prompt: In frame 4, what is the full request URI, including its query string?
hints: Expand Hypertext Transfer Protocol in frame 4.
The URI starts with /checkin and includes ?host=… .
tasks.explanation: Frame 4 is GET /checkin?host=lab-01. Host is a separate header, not part of this URI field.
tasks.feedback: Copy the complete Request URI, including the query after ?. Preserve its case and omit the Host header.

tasks.prompt: Independently locate the third HTTP request. What is its frame number?
hints: Clear the stream filter and apply http.request.
Read the No. column for the last displayed request.
tasks.explanation: Frame 8 is the third request; frame 9 is its response.
tasks.feedback: Apply http.request and read the No. column for the third request. Use the original frame number, not its position in the filtered list.

tasks.prompt: What is the interval in seconds between consecutive HTTP requests? Write only the number.
hints: Compare request times, excluding the handshake.
Subtract frame 4 time from frame 6 time; then verify frames 6 and 8.
tasks.explanation: Request UTC times are 00:00:01, 00:00:31 and 00:01:01 on 1 November 2026. Each gap is 30 seconds.
tasks.feedback: Compare request timestamps, not response times or the handshake. Subtract each request time from the next and enter seconds only.

tasks.prompt: Write a 100–150 word incident summary. Include the hosts, frames, request URI, timing, a cautious inference and the next evidence you would seek. Then self-review it.
hints: Look at the related base word and the sentence meaning.
Keep the base spelling and check the ending letter by letter.
tasks.explanation: A sound report separates captured facts from the automated-polling hypothesis. Neither HTTP 200 nor regular timing establishes compromise.
tasks.example: In this synthetic capture, 192.0.2.10 sends three HTTP GET requests to 198.51.100.20:80. Frames 4, 6 and 8 request /checkin?host=lab-01 with Host: telemetry.lab.test. They occur at 00:00:01, 00:00:31 and 00:01:01 UTC on 1 November 2026, a 30-second interval. The server replies with status 200 and a short plain-text response. The repeated pattern is consistent with automated polling. It does not establish malware infection, process identity or data theft. The capture is a short simulation, so conclusions are limited to these exchanges. I would check endpoint process ownership and relevant logs before escalating the event or deciding whether to contain the host.
rubric: State the 30-second interval with UTC times or equivalent evidence.
Label automated polling as an inference; do not assert proven malware.
Propose endpoint process/log checks and mention the synthetic, limited scope.
languageChecklist: Use 100–150 words as a writing target, not an automatic technical pass.
Use clear past or present tense consistently.
Spell connection, detection and protection carefully if you use them.
Use evidence phrases such as “the capture shows” and “is consistent with”.
tasks.feedback: Use the technical rubric and language checklist. Non-empty writing does not establish a correct investigation.

tasks.prompt: Can this PCAP alone prove malware infection? Answer yes or no.
hints: Separate the captured behaviour from its possible cause.
Legitimate software can also poll a server.
tasks.explanation: No. Regular HTTP check-ins are observable; malicious intent and process identity require more evidence.
tasks.feedback: Consider what process and intent information is absent. Ordinary monitoring can also send regular requests.
